strengths: Novel and timely contribution: extends the generative classifier paradigm beyond diffusion models to VAR models, providing a genuinely new perspective and addressing a real scalability bottleneck (diffusion-based generative classifiers require dozens-hundreds of forward passes).

The proposed techniques (likelihood smoothing and partial-scale candidate pruning) are well-motivated with clear empirical justification (e.g., Fig. 1 showing token instability under imperceptible noise, Fig. 2 showing early-scale sufficiency for coarse discrimination) and are validated via a clean ablation study (Table 2).
Strong practical result: A-VARC+ achieves near-parity accuracy with diffusion classifiers (within 1%) while being ~160x faster, which is a meaningful efficiency contribution.

Honest and nuanced empirical findings: the paper does not oversell robustness, explicitly reporting that VAR-based classifiers do NOT inherit the distribution-shift robustness seen in diffusion classifiers, which is valuable negative evidence for the field's understanding of generative classifiers.

Introduces a novel, cheap (two-forward-pass) visual explainability method (token-wise mutual information / contrastive PMI) that is a natural and elegant extension of pointwise mutual information to the multi-scale VAR framework, with convincing qualitative visualizations including failure case analysis (Fig. 7).

Demonstrates a useful and generalizable insight (independent per-class likelihood modeling gives inherent resistance to catastrophic forgetting) with a proof-of-concept experiment, and thoughtfully discusses the generative/discriminative trade-off as model scale increases (Appendix C/Table 4), which is a candid limitation analysis rather than a hidden one.
Reasonable reproducibility effort: pseudocode, explicit class lists/WordNet IDs, and links to base repositories are provided.
weaknesses: Evaluation is restricted to ImageNet-100 (and small 100-class subsets of shift datasets with only 10 samples/class), despite the paper's stated motivation being scalability to full-scale datasets like ImageNet-1k; no full ImageNet-1k results are shown to substantiate the scalability claim at the scale the introduction emphasizes.

The comparison between A-VARC+ (VAR-d16) and the diffusion classifier (DiT-XL/2) conflates architecture/model-capacity differences with the VAR-vs-diffusion generative-classifier-family comparison, making it harder to cleanly attribute observed property differences (e.g., lack of robustness) to the modeling paradigm rather than to model scale/backbone choice.

The class-incremental learning experiment (Table 3) is a very small-scale proof-of-concept (10 classes, 2 tasks, one baseline CWR), which is insufficient to strongly support the claimed general resistance to catastrophic forgetting compared to established CIL benchmarks/baselines.

Despite the paper's introduction emphasizing adversarial robustness as a hallmark advantage of generative classifiers, no adversarial robustness experiments are conducted; only natural distribution-shift datasets are evaluated.

On ImageNet-A, while A-VARC+ modestly beats ResNet variants, it still substantially underperforms ViT-B/16 and ViT-L/16, which weakens the robustness narrative and is somewhat glossed over in the discussion.

Explainability claims rely solely on qualitative visualizations without any quantitative evaluation (e.g., localization accuracy against bounding boxes/segmentation masks, or human evaluation), limiting the rigor of the explainability contribution.

The appendix analysis (Table 4) reveals that classification accuracy degrades substantially as VAR model size increases (contrary to typical scaling trends), which is an important limitation for future scalability of the approach but is only briefly discussed in the appendix rather than the main text.

The core technical contributions (likelihood smoothing, candidate pruning, applying existing CCA finetuning) are relatively incremental/engineering-oriented adaptations of known techniques rather than fundamentally new methodological insights.

strengths: First systematic exploration of visual autoregressive (VAR) models as generative classifiers, providing a novel complementary perspective to the diffusion-classifier literature.

The proposed A-VARC/A-VARC+ techniques (likelihood smoothing, partial-scale candidate pruning, CCA finetuning) are reasonably motivated and yield a substantial (160x) speedup over diffusion classifiers with modest accuracy loss on ImageNet-100.

Token-wise mutual information for visual explainability is a neat, cheap-to-compute extension of PMI to the multi-scale VAR setting and produces intuitive qualitative visualizations (including informative failure-case analysis).
The class-incremental learning experiment, while small, illustrates a plausible qualitative advantage of generative classifiers over naively finetuned discriminative baselines.

Reasonably thorough comparison across multiple distribution-shift benchmarks (ImageNetV2/R/Sketch/A, ObjectNet) and against both generative and discriminative baselines, with details provided for reproducibility.
weaknesses: All main experiments are conducted on ImageNet-100 (and small 10-sample-per-class subsets of shift datasets), despite the paper's motivating narrative being about scalability to large numbers of classes (e.g., full ImageNet-1k); no results are shown at the scale that would actually stress-test the claimed efficiency advantage.

The reported accuracy gap to discriminative classifiers remains large (e.g., 89.32% A-VARC+ vs. 94.20% ViT-B/16, and generative classifiers underperform discriminative ones on essentially every distribution-shift dataset), so the practical value proposition is unclear beyond matching a slower diffusion baseline.

A central motivating claim of generative classifiers (robustness to distribution shift) is shown NOT to transfer to the VAR setting in this paper's own experiments, undermining much of the premise built up in the introduction/related work; the paper pivots post hoc to explainability/incremental learning as the 'real' contributions.

Appendix C reveals that classification accuracy degrades substantially as the underlying VAR model scales up (better FID, worse accuracy), suggesting the proposed classifier does not benefit from — and may be fundamentally at odds with — future improvements in VAR generative quality, which is a serious scalability/future-proofing concern that is acknowledged but not resolved.

CCA finetuning, a core component of A-VARC+, is shown to hurt OOD generalization (ImageNet-A, ImageNet-Sketch) in the ablation, indicating the accuracy gains are partly an in-distribution overfitting effect rather than a genuine improvement in class-conditional modeling.

Techniques are largely adaptations of existing ideas from other domains/papers (reweighted discriminative terms from Fetaya et al./Mackowiak et al., CCA from Chen et al. 2024b, PMI from NLP, candidate pruning analogous to Li et al. 2023's two-stage ELBO approach), limiting technical novelty.

The class-incremental learning experiment is a minimal proof of concept (10 classes, 2 tasks, 5 classes each) with a weak discriminative baseline comparison (no rehearsal vs. only CWR), which is not convincing evidence of a general property; stronger continual learning baselines (EWC, iCaRL, etc.) are not considered.

Explainability claims are supported only by qualitative heatmap examples without any quantitative evaluation (e.g., localization/insertion-deletion metrics, comparison to Grad-CAM or other established explanation baselines on the same images), making it hard to assess rigor or advantage over existing XAI methods.
Runtime comparisons for diffusion classifiers are only 'estimated' on a single A6000 from heterogeneous hardware, which weakens the precision of the headline 160x speedup claim.

strengths: Introduces a novel and timely application of VAR models as generative classifiers, broadening a research area that has been narrowly focused on diffusion-based approaches, and the paper provides a genuinely new perspective by comparing properties across model families.

The proposed techniques (likelihood smoothing and partial-scale candidate pruning) are well motivated with clear empirical illustrations (e.g., Fig.1 showing token sensitivity to imperceptible perturbations, Fig.2 showing accuracy/efficiency trade-off across scales), and ablations (Table 2) cleanly isolate the contribution of each component.
Strong practical result: A-VARC+ achieves near-parity accuracy with diffusion classifiers while being ~160x faster, which is a meaningful step toward making generative classifiers practically usable.

The extension of pointwise mutual information to token-wise mutual information for visual explainability is a nice, intuitive idea that leverages the tractable likelihood of VAR models, and is illustrated with both successful and failure-case qualitative examples.

The finding that VAR-based generative classifiers are resistant to catastrophic forgetting in class-incremental learning is interesting and practically relevant, offering a lightweight alternative to rehearsal-based methods.

The paper is scientifically honest in reporting a negative result (the OOD robustness advantage of diffusion classifiers does not transfer to VAR), which adds credibility and nuance to the claimed contributions.
Good reproducibility effort: class subsets, pseudocode, and implementation details are provided in the appendix.
The appendix analysis on the generative/discriminative trade-off as model size increases (Table 4, Fig.4) adds useful depth and sets up a concrete direction for future work.
weaknesses: Evaluation is restricted to ImageNet-100 and small subsets (10 samples/class) for distribution-shift datasets, which limits the strength of claims about scalability and robustness; full ImageNet-1k results (even if only for the efficient A-VARC+ method) would substantially strengthen the scalability claim.

The class-incremental learning experiment is very small-scale (10 classes, 2 tasks, no standard CIL benchmarks like CIFAR-100 splits or longer task sequences) and reads more as a proof-of-concept than a rigorous evaluation; comparison to more CIL baselines beyond CWR would help.

Visual explainability claims rely solely on qualitative examples; no quantitative evaluation (e.g., localization/pointing-game accuracy, deletion-insertion AUC, or human evaluation) is provided to substantiate that the token-wise mutual information faithfully reflects class-relevant regions.

The generative-classifier baselines compared against are limited (IBINN and one diffusion classifier variant); comparison to other recent diffusion/ELBO-based classifiers or other autoregressive baselines would make the comparative analysis more comprehensive.

CCA finetuning improves in-distribution accuracy but reduces robustness on ImageNet-A/Sketch, and this trade-off is not deeply analyzed or resolved, leaving the benefit of the '+' version somewhat mixed.

Runtime comparisons for diffusion baselines are estimated/normalized across heterogeneous hardware rather than measured directly, which introduces some uncertainty into the headline 160x speedup claim.

The three-stage pipeline involves several hyperparameters (K', number of stages, S, sigma) that appear empirically tuned for this specific setup without a thorough sensitivity analysis or theoretical justification for the chosen configuration generalizing to other datasets/model scales.

strengths: Novel investigation of VAR-based generative classifiers, extending the generative classifier literature beyond the diffusion-based models that have dominated recent work, and providing a genuinely new perspective (tractable likelihood vs. ELBO approximation).

Strong efficiency gains: A-VARC+ achieves accuracy within ~1% of the 2-stage DiT-based diffusion classifier while requiring ~89x less computation, which is a meaningful practical contribution given the scalability bottleneck of generative classifiers.

The two core techniques (likelihood smoothing to address non-smooth token-map likelihoods, and partial-scale candidate pruning exploiting the coarse-to-fine VAR structure) are well-motivated by clear empirical observations (e.g., Fig. 1's token instability under imperceptible perturbation, Fig. 2's scale-vs-accuracy curve) and are validated with thorough ablations (Tables 2, 5, 6, and Appendix B).

The application of CCA finetuning to boost class-conditional signal is a sensible adaptation of a recent technique, and the paper honestly reports its trade-off (helps in-domain accuracy, slightly hurts distribution-shift generalization).

Interesting and largely novel findings on token-wise mutual information (TMI) for visual explainability, including contrastive explanations, evaluated quantitatively against LIME/SHAP with insertion/deletion metrics, not just qualitative figures.

The class-incremental learning study and the model-scale trade-off analysis (Appendix D, showing larger VAR models dilute class information and hurt discriminative accuracy despite better FID) add depth and additional useful negative/nuanced findings rather than only positive results.
Reasonably transparent reporting of negative results (VAR classifiers do not inherit diffusion models' distribution-shift robustness), which strengthens scientific credibility.
Good reproducibility support: code release promised, detailed algorithm pseudocode, and explicit listing of dataset subsets/class splits in the appendix.
weaknesses: Main robustness/distribution-shift evaluations use very small samples (10 images per class, and only 100-113 classes), which raises concerns about the statistical reliability of the reported accuracy differences, especially since no variance/confidence intervals are reported.

The class-incremental learning experiment is a small proof-of-concept (only 10 ImageNet classes split into 2 tasks of 5 classes each, single run, no averaging over multiple task orderings or seeds), which is insufficient to strongly support the claimed advantage of generative classifiers for class-incremental learning at scale.

Primary comparative evaluation is restricted to ImageNet-100; the paper does not evaluate on full ImageNet-1000, so the central scalability claim (motivated explicitly by the ImageNet-1000 scale) is not directly demonstrated at the scale that matters most.

The core technical contributions (Gaussian smoothing of likelihoods, coarse-to-fine candidate pruning, borrowing CCA from a concurrent paper) are individually relatively straightforward adaptations of existing ideas to a new backbone, somewhat limiting the technical novelty of the framework itself.

The token-masking procedure used for LIME/SHAP/TMI quantitative evaluation relies on a precomputed log-likelihood masking approximation rather than actually removing tokens and re-running the model, which may not faithfully reflect the true causal effect of token removal and could bias the insertion/deletion comparison in TMI's favor.

Despite the title's emphasis on VAR classifiers being broadly "efficient and explainable," the reported accuracy still trails standard discriminative classifiers by several points across nearly all datasets (Table 1), and the paper acknowledges generative classifiers remain far from closing this gap, somewhat tempering the practical significance of the contribution.

The paper's key selling point (89x speed-up) is measured against the diffusion classifier's default many-sample configuration; a more apples-to-apples comparison at matched compute budgets for both approaches would make the efficiency claims more convincing.

strengths: Investigates an underexplored and timely direction: using VAR's tractable likelihood as a far more efficient alternative to diffusion-based generative classifiers, addressing a real scalability bottleneck in prior work.

Solid engineering package (likelihood smoothing, partial-scale candidate pruning, CCA finetuning) that empirically yields large efficiency gains (~89x fewer GFLOPs) with only ~1% accuracy drop relative to a 2-stage DiT diffusion classifier on ImageNet-100.

Introduces token-wise mutual information (TMI) as a natural extension of PMI for autoregressive models, providing an interpretable, contrastive visual explanation method with only two forward passes; quantitatively benchmarked against LIME/SHAP using insertion/deletion metrics.

Reasonably broad empirical analysis spanning five distribution-shift datasets, ablations on smoothing sample count and variance, and a model-scale trade-off study (Appendix D) showing an interesting dilution-of-class-information effect as VAR model size grows.

Honest and nuanced reporting of negative findings (e.g., VAR-based classifiers do not inherit diffusion models' distribution-shift robustness), which adds scientific value by tempering over-generalized claims about generative classifiers.
weaknesses: Despite framing scalability to large-class datasets as the central motivation, the main comparative results are limited to ImageNet-100; no full ImageNet-1k experiments are shown, leaving the core scalability claim only partially substantiated.

Absolute accuracy remains clearly below discriminative baselines (89.32% vs. 94.20% for ViT-B/16) and also trails the full diffusion classifier on several robustness datasets, so the practical case for adopting this generative classifier over standard discriminative or even diffusion-based alternatives is not strongly made.

The class-incremental learning study is a very small proof-of-concept (10 classes, 2 tasks of 5 classes), with only one CIL baseline (CWR) and no comparison to established generative-classifier CIL results at larger scale; this undercuts the strength of the claimed CIL advantage.

Technical novelty is somewhat incremental: candidate pruning is directly inspired by the diffusion classifier's two-stage approach, and CCA is adopted wholesale from prior work (Chen et al., 2024b) rather than developed in this paper; the main original components (likelihood smoothing, partial-scale pruning) are relatively simple engineering tweaks.

Explainability results are mixed rather than uniformly favorable—LIME outperforms TMI on both metrics for the non-finetuned A-VARC, and TMI only becomes competitive after CCA finetuning—weakening the claim that tractable likelihood 'inherently' provides strong explainability.

The three-stage pipeline (K, S, σ, and which likelihood estimator to use at each stage) introduces multiple hyperparameters whose selection appears largely empirical/ad hoc rather than principled, raising reproducibility and generalization concerns across datasets/backbones.

Reported efficiency numbers (GFLOPs) do not clearly account for the added CCA finetuning cost, which is non-trivial and would affect a fair end-to-end efficiency comparison against baselines that do not require such finetuning.

strengths: Novel and timely research direction: extends generative classifiers to VAR models, a largely unexplored backbone compared to VAE/flow/diffusion-based prior work.
Strong efficiency-accuracy trade-off is well demonstrated: A-VARC+ achieves comparable accuracy to DiT-based diffusion classifiers with ~89x less computation, which is a compelling practical result.

The two core technical contributions (likelihood smoothing and partial-scale candidate pruning) are well motivated with clear empirical justification (e.g., the token-flip experiment in Fig. 1, and the scale-vs-accuracy curve in Fig. 2).

Creative extension of pointwise mutual information to token-wise mutual information (TMI) for visual explainability, validated both qualitatively (heatmaps) and quantitatively (insertion/deletion AUC against LIME/SHAP baselines).
Interesting and underexplored finding on natural class-incremental learning without replay, supported by a controlled comparison against discriminative models and CWR.

The paper is scientifically honest: it explicitly reports that the distribution-shift robustness seen in diffusion-based generative classifiers does not transfer to VAR, rather than overselling positive results.
Comprehensive appendix ablations (varying S, variance σ, model size trade-offs between generative/discriminative performance) add depth and support reproducibility understanding.
weaknesses: Evaluation is restricted to ImageNet-100 (and 100-class subsets of shift datasets) rather than the full 1000-class ImageNet, which is the primary scalability challenge motivating the paper; it remains unclear how well A-VARC+ scales to the full label space the introduction emphasizes.

Distribution-shift experiments use only 10 samples per class, which raises concerns about the statistical reliability of the reported accuracy differences, especially for smaller shift datasets like ImageNet-A/ObjectNet.

While A-VARC+ is far cheaper than diffusion classifiers, it still requires orders of magnitude more compute than discriminative baselines (e.g., 4649 GFLOPs vs. 1.8–60 GFLOPs for ResNet/ViT), so the "efficient" framing should be more carefully contextualized relative to discriminative classifiers, not only diffusion ones.

The CCA finetuning component that forms A-VARC+ is adopted largely as-is from prior work (Chen et al. 2024b), somewhat limiting the technical novelty of this specific sub-contribution relative to the paper's other original pieces (smoothing, pruning, TMI).
The class-incremental learning experiment is very small scale (only 10 classes split into 2 tasks of 5), limiting the strength of the generalization claims about avoiding catastrophic forgetting.

Explainability results are mixed: TMI underperforms LIME on the base A-VARC model (Table 3), which somewhat weakens the claim of inherent superior explainability, even though it wins after CCA finetuning.
No public code link is provided at submission time (placeholder repository), limiting ability to verify reproducibility during review despite detailed appendix descriptions.
Additional diverse datasets beyond ImageNet-family variants (e.g., finer-grained or non-natural image domains) would strengthen generality claims of the proposed generative classifier framework.
